description: SmartCollective is a team of four passionate developers focused on creating smart, user-friendly solutions. Using Flutter, we combine creativity, technology, and problem-solving to tackle real-world challenges. In the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to build an innovative, practical, and impactful prototype.
summary: Orbit is a health monitoring prototype that helps users record measurements, review trends, and compare resting heart rate with a dynamic personal baseline. Its initial business opportunity is serving space mission simulation centers and research teams through institutional subscriptions. Future versions could support remote workplaces, including research stations and offshore facilities. Revenue could come from subscriptions, customization, device integration, and technical support. The expected value is better organized records and easier review by medical teams. Pilot studies must demonstrate usability, data completeness, and time savings. Orbit currently uses manual input and requires further security development and clinical evaluation before deployment.
details:
Orbit is a bilingual health monitoring prototype designed to help astronauts record and understand changes in their health during long space missions. It brings measurements, historical trends, and measurement context together in one interface.

Users manually record heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep duration, and mood. They also specify the mission phase, whether the measurement was taken at rest or after exercise, and whether symptoms were present. Orbit checks inputs, stores records locally, and displays trends across 7, 30, or 90 days. Missing measurements remain identified as missing.

Our main feature is the Dynamic Personal Baseline, currently implemented for resting heart rate. Rather than relying only on general ranges, Orbit compares each person with their own measurement history. After seven eligible days, it establishes an initial reference using daily median values. It then updates gradually using an exponentially weighted moving average with a weighting factor of 0.1. Using one median per day prevents repeated measurements from giving that day excessive influence.

The system preserves the initial phase reference, excludes unsuitable readings from updates, and includes experimental safeguards against excessive drift. These settings are engineering choices for the prototype, not NASA-prescribed or clinically validated thresholds. A changing baseline does not establish that a change represents healthy adaptation.

Orbit’s intended benefit is clearer, more organized health information for users and eventual review by medical teams. Its expected impact is to make changes easier to notice and discuss, particularly when access to medical support is difficult. These benefits still require evaluation through user studies and appropriate clinical assessment.

We developed Orbit using Flutter and Dart, with local storage through shared preferences. GitHub manages the source code, and GitHub Actions builds and publishes the web application through GitHub Pages. No dedicated hardware is required for the current browser demonstration. Measurements are entered manually, and demonstration data is simulated. An optional COSMO educational assistant uses a Node.js proxy to keep its API key outside the Flutter client; it requires connectivity and does not control baseline calculations.

The project’s creative contribution is the combination of personal comparisons, gradual reference updates, measurement context, and a preserved starting reference. This helps communicate both recent patterns and longer-term differences.

Our team considered NASA’s five human spaceflight hazards, Canadian Space Agency resources, limited connectivity, data quality, Arabic and English accessibility, and the risk of misleading interpretations. Future development includes secure synchronization, real authentication, medical review tools, and integration with validated measurement devices. Orbit remains a monitoring prototype, not a diagnostic system or a replacement for medical care.
